[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/6dice%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-6dice%28cropped%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:6dice(cropped).jpg)

A typical set of polyhedral dice in various colors. They consist of the five Platonic solids, along with a ten-sided die that is also used for generating percentages.

Various shapes such as two-sided or four-sided dice are documented in archaeological findings; for example, from Ancient Egypt and the Middle East. While the cubical six-sided die became the most common type in many parts of the world, other shapes were always known, like 20-sided dice in Ptolemaic and Roman times.

The modern tradition of using *sets* of polyhedral dice started around the end of the 1960s when non-cubical dice became popular among players of [wargames](/wiki/Wargame "Wargame"),[[32]](#cite_note-Peterson2012-32) and since have been employed extensively in [role-playing games](/wiki/Role-playing_game "Role-playing game") and [trading card games](/wiki/Collectible_card_game "Collectible card game"). Dice using both the numerals 6 and 9, which are reciprocally symmetric through rotation, typically distinguish them with a dot or underline.

Some twenty-sided dice have a different arrangement used for the purpose of keeping track of an integer that counts down, such as health points. These *spindown dice* are arranged such that adjacent integers appear on adjacent faces, allowing the user to easily find the next lower number. They are commonly used with [collectible card games](/wiki/Collectible_card_game "Collectible card game").[[33]](#cite_note-33)

In September 2004, the professional Japanese players went on strike for the first time in over 70 years. The owners wanted to get rid of the financially defunct Buffaloes, and merge the two baseball leagues, since teams in the [Central League](/wiki/Central_League "Central League") saw much higher profits than the [Pacific League](/wiki/Pacific_League "Pacific League"), having popular teams such as the [Yomiuri Giants](/wiki/Yomiuri_Giants "Yomiuri Giants") and [Hanshin Tigers](/wiki/Hanshin_Tigers "Hanshin Tigers"). After negotiations, the owners agreed to guarantee the survival of the [Chiba Lotte Marines](/wiki/Chiba_Lotte_Marines "Chiba Lotte Marines") and the [Fukuoka Daiei Hawks](/wiki/Fukuoka_Daiei_Hawks "Fukuoka Daiei Hawks"), leaving the Central League with six teams and the Pacific League with five.

A battle escalated between the players union and the owners, and reached its height when Yomiuri Giants owner [Tsuneo Watanabe](/wiki/Tsuneo_Watanabe "Tsuneo Watanabe") controversially remarked that Furuta was "a mere player",[[29]](#cite_note-29) implying that players had no say in what league would look like the next year. The dispute received huge press coverage (which mostly favored Furuta and the players' union) and was dubbed one of the biggest events in the history of Japanese baseball. Obasanjo had been in prison under the dictatorship of Abacha. Obasanjo's inauguration heralded the beginning of the Fourth Nigerian Republic,[[90]](#cite_note-92) ending a 39-year period of short-lived democracies, civil war and military dictatorship. Although the elections that brought Obasanjo to power and allowed him to run for a second term in the 2003 presidential elections were condemned as unfree and unfair, Nigeria made significant progress in democratisation under Obasanjo.[[91]](#cite_note-93)

NATO was established on 4 April 1949 via the signing of the [North Atlantic Treaty](/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty "North Atlantic Treaty") (Washington Treaty). In addition to the 12 founding countries, four new members joined during the Cold War: [Greece](/wiki/Greece "Greece") and [Turkey](/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") (1952), [West Germany](/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") (1955) and [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain") (1982). Additionally, NATO experienced territorial expansion during this period without adding new member states when [Zone A of the Free Territory of Trieste](/wiki/Free_Territory_of_Trieste#Dissolution "Free Territory of Trieste") was annexed by Italy in 1954, and the territory of the former [East Germany](/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") was added with the [reunification of Germany](/wiki/German_reunification "German reunification") in 1990. Spain have won the most UEFA European Championships, with four titles.[[108]](#cite_note-110) *La Roja* are also the only nation to date to have won consecutive championships. They have hosted the tournament once, in [1964](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1964 "UEFA Euro 1964") (one city was used to host games at [Euro 2020](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2020 "UEFA Euro 2020")) and have appeared in a total of twelve tournaments.

The team won their first international trophy on home soil in 1964, defeating the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union_national_football_team "Soviet Union national football team") 2–1.[[109]](#cite_note-111)[[110]](#cite_note-112) Spain would reach the final twenty years later in [1984](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1984_final "UEFA Euro 1984 final"), where they would lose the final to [France](/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team"). Spain would not reach the final again until [2008](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2008_final "UEFA Euro 2008 final"), where they would defeat Germany 1–0. Four years later, Spain earned back-to-back titles, comprehensively defeating [Italy](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team") 4–0 in the [final](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2012_final "UEFA Euro 2012 final") in Kyiv.

It would take *La Roja* twelve years to reach another European final, doing so in [2024](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2024_final "UEFA Euro 2024 final") against [England](/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team"), a match they won 2–1 to stand alone as the most successful national team in the competition's history with four titles, while at the same time becoming the first team ever to win all seven matches in a single tournament.[[111]](#cite_note-113)
